results.claim: The fixed-k problems are monotone under padding: k-Induced Disjoint Paths reduces to ℓ-Induced Disjoint Paths for every fixed ℓ≥k while preserving H3-freeness. Moreover, k=1 is linear-time solvable and every fixed-k problem is in NP.
results.proof_sketch: Given an instance with k pairs, add ℓ−k disjoint K2 components and use each new edge as a terminal pair. Since H3 is connected, the enlarged graph is H3-free exactly when the original graph is. Every new pair has its unique path, so the enlarged instance is equivalent to the original one. Consequently, hardness propagates upward in k, while an algorithm for ℓ yields algorithms for all smaller k. For k=1, a solution exists exactly when its two terminals are connected: a shortest connecting path is induced. For fixed k, the k paths form a polynomial-size certificate whose vertex-disjointness and absence of inter-path edges can be checked directly.

results.claim: Every H3-free graph is 6-degenerate, with the constant sharp; additionally, two vertices of degree at least three can never be at distance exactly three. Thus an n-vertex H3-free graph has at most 6n−21 edges for n≥7, and every connected H3-free graph of minimum degree at least three has diameter at most two.
results.proof_sketch:
Let u-x-y-v be a shortest path of length three with deg(u),deg(v)≥3. Vertex u has two neighbors other than x, and v has two neighbors other than y. These four neighbors lie outside the central path. The two pairs are disjoint, since a common neighbor would give a u-v path of length two. They therefore supply the four leaves of H3, a contradiction. The diameter consequence follows by taking the first four vertices of any geodesic of length at least three.

For degeneracy, every graph of minimum degree at least seven contains every eight-vertex tree: root the tree and embed vertices parent-first; when embedding the jth vertex, its embedded parent has at most j−2≤6 previously used possible neighbors and at least seven neighbors in total. Hence a graph having a subgraph of minimum degree seven contains H3. An H3-free graph is therefore 6-degenerate. A degeneracy ordering gives the stated edge bound. K7 is H3-free because H3 has eight vertices, and K7 has degeneracy six.

results.claim: H3-free graphs admit an arbitrary-routing-plus-matching normal form. Let R be any graph and M a matching on V(R), disjoint from E(R). Replace every edge of R by a four-edge path and retain every edge of M unsubdivided, obtaining G(R,M). Then G(R,M) is H3-free. With all terminals in V(R), induced linkages in G(R,M) correspond exactly to vertex-disjoint paths in R∪M such that every M-edge whose two endpoints are selected is itself used between consecutive vertices of one path. In particular, the H3-free class has unbounded treewidth.
results.proof_sketch:
All new subdivision vertices have degree two, so the two degree-three centers of a putative H3 must both be original vertices. A simple path beginning along a subdivided R-edge needs four edges to reach another original vertex. If it begins with an M-edge, the matching property prevents taking a second M-edge, and the remaining two steps along a subdivided R-edge end at a subdivision vertex. Thus no three-edge path joins two possible centers.

A path with original endpoints must traverse every used subdivided R-edge completely, so contracting these four-edge paths projects it to a simple path in R∪M, and this operation is reversible. Subdivided R-edges cause neither chords nor edges between vertex-disjoint lifted paths. The only possible extra adjacencies are unsubdivided M-edges. Such an adjacency is allowed exactly when it is used consecutively within one path, proving the correspondence. Taking M empty and R=K_m gives a four-subdivision of K_m. It contains K_m as a minor, so its treewidth is at least m−1 although it is H3-free.

results.claim: Conditional contraction lemma: if R and M are supplied, M is a matching on V(R) disjoint from E(R), G=G(R,M), and all terminals are distinct vertices of V(R), then preprocessing matching edges with two terminal endpoints and contracting every remaining edge of M reduces induced linkage in G exactly to ordinary vertex-disjoint linkage in a quotient graph. Consequently, for every fixed k this represented-input, original-terminal problem is polynomial-time solvable.
results.proof_sketch:
Apply the preceding correspondence in X=R∪M. If xy∈M joins terminals from different prescribed pairs, both endpoints must lie on different paths, violating matching-cleanliness, so reject. If {x,y} is a prescribed pair, matching-cleanliness forces its path to be xy; remove that pair and its endpoints. Every remaining M-edge has at most one terminal. Contract those edges in X, simplify parallel edges, and map each terminal to its contraction class, producing Q.

A matching-clean linkage contracts to vertex-disjoint simple paths in Q, since selecting both ends of a matched pair nonconsecutively or on different paths is forbidden. Conversely, choose for each quotient-path edge an originating R-edge. At a visited matched class, use one endpoint when the two incident chosen edges use the same port, and insert its M-edge when they use opposite ports; at a terminal class, start at the actual terminal and insert the M-edge exactly if needed to reach the first port. Disjoint quotient paths visit disjoint classes, so their lifts are vertex-disjoint and matching-clean. Expanding used R-edges gives an induced linkage in G. To solve Q for fixed k using only the source-stated result, four-subdivide every Q-edge. This graph is H1-subgraph-free, and induced linkages in it correspond exactly to ordinary linkages in Q.

results.claim: The conditional contraction lemma does not establish polynomial-time solvability for standard instances on the entire graph class {G(R,M)}: a standard instance supplies only G, may put terminals at subdivision vertices, and need not determine a unique R,M representation. Therefore the classification for every fixed k≥2 remains open in this draft.
results.proof_sketch: For terminal scope, a four-edge subdivision a0-a1-a2-a3-a4 of K2 is G(R,∅), but terminals a1 and a3 are subdivision vertices and disappear from the projected graph R∪M; using two disjoint copies supplies four distinct internal terminals for a 2-instance. Thus the proved quotient map is undefined for allowed standard instances. For representation scope, the same labeled P6 has a description with 0-1-2-3-4 as an R-corridor and 4-5 as an M-edge, and another with 0-1 as an M-edge and 1-2-3-4-5 as an R-corridor. Hence M is not determined by G. These examples do not prove that recognition or full-class solution is impossible; they show that neither is supplied by the conditional reduction. Since the remaining results give no full-class polynomial algorithm or NP-hardness proof for any fixed k≥2, the source target is not resolved.

results.claim: Four is the sharp universal corridor length in the arbitrary-routing-plus-matching construction: replacing every R-edge by a path of any fixed length d≥4 always produces an H3-free graph after retaining M, whereas each d∈{1,2,3} has a permitted pair (R,M) whose resulting graph contains H3.
results.proof_sketch:
For d≥4, an H3 center must be original because every subdivision vertex has degree two. If a three-edge center path starts along an R-corridor, three steps do not reach another original vertex. If it starts with an M-edge, the matching condition prevents a second M-edge; its remaining two steps enter an R-corridor and again do not reach an original vertex.

For d=1, take R=H3 and M empty. For d=3, take R=K4 and M empty: any subdivided R-edge is the three-edge center path, while the first subdivision vertices on the other two incident corridors at each endpoint provide the four leaves. For d=2, use distinct originals u,v,w,p,q,r,s, let E(R)={up,uq,vw,wr,ws}, and let M={uv}. If a subdivides vw, then u-v-a-w is a three-edge center path; the first subdivision vertices on up, uq, wr, and ws are its four leaves. Thus every smaller uniform length fails in an allowed instance.

results.claim: For arbitrary graphs, hence also for H3-free graphs, k-Induced Disjoint Paths is fixed-parameter tractable in k+b, where b is the number of vertices of degree at least three. There is an exact equivalent compression with at most b+binom(b,2)+6k vertices.
results.proof_sketch:
Let B contain the b vertices of degree at least three. Every component of G−B is a path, isolated vertex, or cycle and has at most two attachment edges. A terminal-free component can participate only as a corridor between two distinct B vertices; same-end and dead-end components cannot occur in a simple terminal path. Corridors with the same unordered endpoints are interchangeable because their internal vertices have no other neighbors, so retain one two-edge representative per pair.

In a terminal-bearing component, order its terminals and B-attachment occurrences along the path or cycle; the same B vertex may occur at both ends. Between consecutive marks is an unmarked gap. Every solution either avoids or completely traverses each gap. Preserve a one-edge gap and replace every longer gap by a two-edge path, retaining endpoint adjacency, liftability, vertex-disjointness, chords, and inter-path adjacencies. A detached cycle containing exactly one terminal is an immediate NO case and is handled separately. A terminal-bearing path component with t terminals has at most t+1≤2t gaps, while a cycle has t gaps. Thus there are at most b+2k marked vertices, binom(b,2) generic representatives, and 4k gap representatives. Exhaustive path enumeration in the compressed graph depends only on k+b, and every compressed solution lifts polynomially, proving FPT.

results.claim: A globally shortest path for one terminal pair cannot be fixed greedily, even on a seven-vertex H3-free graph.
results.proof_sketch: Use vertices s1,t1,x,s2,t2,y,z and edges s1x, xt1, xs2, s2t2, s1y, yz, zt1. The graph is H3-free because it has only seven vertices. The paths s1-y-z-t1 and s2-t2 form a valid induced linkage. However, s1-x-t1 is the unique shortest s1-t1 path, and its vertex x is adjacent to s2; hence it is incompatible with every s2-t2 path. Thus replacing one member of a solution by a globally shortest path is not a valid reduction rule.

results.claim: The seven-vertex obstruction is vertex-minimal for the unique-shortest formulation and also defeats total-length minimization: no graph on at most six vertices with four distinct terminals has an induced linkage while the first pair's unique globally shortest path is unextendable, and in the seven-vertex witness the unique minimum-total-length ordinary two-linkage is not induced.
results.proof_sketch:
Suppose P1,P2 form an induced linkage and the unique shortest s1-t1 path Q cannot extend with the second pair. Since Q differs from P1, it is strictly shorter. P1 must have at least three edges: if it had one there would be no shorter path, while if it had two the only shorter possibility would use just s1,t1 and therefore would remain compatible with P2. On at most six vertices, P1 consequently has exactly four vertices, P2 is the edge s2t2, and together they use every vertex. Q cannot be the edge s1t1 for the same compatibility reason, so it has two edges. Its internal vertex is either internal to P1, in which case Q uses a subset of P1's vertices and extends with P2, or belongs to P2, in which case its incident edges are forbidden edges between P1 and P2. Both are contradictions.

In the displayed seven-vertex graph, s2t2 is the only simple s2-t2 path and s1-x-t1 is the unique shortest first path. Their union is therefore the unique minimum-total-length ordinary linkage, but xs2 makes it non-induced; the longer displayed linkage is induced.

final_writeup:
This remains a partial result: it settles k=1 but does not classify k-Induced Disjoint Paths on all H3-subgraph-free graphs for any fixed k≥2. Monotonicity under padding, NP membership, 6-degeneracy and its sharpness, the distance-three restriction on branching vertices, unbounded treewidth, the bounded-branching compression, the sharp corridor length, and the shortest-path obstructions all survive the audit unchanged.

The contraction argument survives only with an explicit input-model restriction. Given R and M as part of the input and requiring every terminal to be an original vertex of R, first reject a matching edge joining terminals from different pairs and fix and remove a matching edge that is itself a prescribed pair. Contract every remaining matching edge in R∪M. Matching-clean projected paths contract to ordinary vertex-disjoint quotient paths. Conversely, quotient paths lift port by port: use one endpoint of a matched class when its incident route edges use the same port, and traverse the matching edge when they use opposite ports. Four-subdivision turns the quotient into an H1-subgraph-free instance, so the source-stated fixed-k polynomial result applies. Thus only the represented-input, original-terminal problem is proved polynomial.

The stronger standard graph-class conclusion is withdrawn. In a standard instance, the input need not identify R or M and terminals may lie inside four-edge corridors. A P5 corridor with internal terminals makes the stated projection undefined, while a labeled P6 has two valid descriptions with different matching edges. The latter does not rule out a representation-recovery algorithm, but none is proved; nor is there a reduction for arbitrary subdivision-vertex terminals. The conditional lemma therefore cannot support polynomial solvability on the entire class of graphs admitting some G(R,M) representation.

The remaining verified results are substantive but do not close the target. Four-subdivisions of cliques show that H3-freeness does not bound treewidth. Compression to at most b+binom(b,2)+6k vertices yields FPT in k+b, but H3-freeness does not bound b. The seven-vertex witness blocks both greedily fixing a globally shortest path and relying on the minimum-total-length ordinary linkage. Accordingly, this draft supplies neither a full-class polynomial algorithm nor an NP-hardness proof for any fixed k≥2, and PARTIAL is the strongest supported resolution.
